frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains leverage through pipeline gas to Italy and Spain, but European diversification and renewable investment gradually reduce its bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign investment controls
frictionVectors.details: Strict ownership rules and regulatory uncertainty protect state control but constrain outside capital and technology in hydrocarbons, mining, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon exposure
frictionVectors.details: Oil still dominates export earnings and fiscal stability, leaving Angola vulnerable to production declines, price shocks, and foreign operator decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European partners, China, and Gulf actors are competing for influence over the corridor linking Angolan ports to critical mineral zones in the DRC and Zambia.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and illicit networks moving south from Burkina Faso and Niger are pressuring Benin's northern security and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's importance to regional trade creates leverage for external financiers and neighboring economies, while infrastructure expansion increases exposure to foreign contractors.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is seeking greater domestic value capture and marketing control in its diamond partnership, balancing sovereignty gains against access to global distribution networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in Botswana's copper, nickel, and other minerals is increasing, creating pressure to secure transparent concessions and prevent excessive foreign control.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization
frictionVectors.details: The junta is expanding state control over gold marketing and mining, but limited technical capacity and informal production leave room for foreign and illicit intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: Jihadist insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Persistent militant control and attacks disrupt mines, roads, and agricultural zones, weakening the state's ability to secure and monetize its resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and rare-metal concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale nickel development is advancing under significant foreign capital and opaque contracting conditions, limiting public oversight of strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–DRC security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Rwanda and instability in eastern DRC constrain border trade, transport access, and Burundi's ability to independently manage regional security.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime-security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, logistics, and maritime-security projects strengthen Cabo Verde's strategic position but create long-term reliance on external operators and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and aid concentration
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on tourism, remittances, and concessional finance leaves the economy exposed to external shocks and limits autonomous resource mobilization.

highlights: Oil, gas, and timber remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Chad–Cameroon pipeline and offshore energy sector tie national revenues and infrastructure to foreign operators, transit arrangements, and fluctuating commodity prices.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and transport bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts roads, agricultural supply chains, and state access while complicating external investment in ports and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security–mining nexus
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security actors has expanded the government's territorial reach but increased concerns over opaque access to gold, diamonds, and other concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Cross-border mineral smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Weak border administration and limited transport infrastructure allow armed groups and regional traders to divert extractive revenues away from state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil exports through Cameroon and foreign technical and financial partners, leaving revenue control vulnerable to external disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan conflict spillover
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan is driving refugee flows, arms trafficking, and militia activity along Chad's eastern frontier, diverting state resources from independent development.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, making territorial sovereignty and migration management a persistent bilateral flashpoint. Comoros has limited leverage despite continued diplomatic claims.

frictionVectors.title: Port and connectivity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic capital leaves transport, telecommunications, and energy infrastructure dependent on foreign donors and contractors, constraining sovereign policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: M23 conflict and regional intervention
frictionVectors.details: The M23 conflict and alleged external backing continue to weaken Kinshasa's control in the east, while Rwanda, Uganda, and international actors shape security outcomes.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals and opaque contracts
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and other minerals attract Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked investment, but weak governance and processing capacity limit the state's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State revenue and export earnings remain heavily dependent on hydrocarbons, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price volatility and external oil-sector influence.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and resource relationships provide essential roads, ports, and financing but can narrow fiscal and negotiating space when debt pressures intensify.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cocoa value chains
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening local processing and pricing institutions, but multinational firms still command major segments of cocoa finance, trading, and processing.

frictionVectors.title: Northern spillover and security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence from the Sahel remains a security risk near northern borders, encouraging continued reliance on foreign intelligence, equipment, and regional security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and leverage but make Djibouti's sovereignty highly dependent on rival external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port debt and Ethiopian dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's logistics economy is tied to Ethiopia's trade corridor and heavily financed infrastructure, while debt exposure and competition with neighboring ports constrain national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on IMF support and Gulf investment constrains fiscal autonomy and gives external partners influence over strategic assets and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Contestation
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains a major sovereignty and water-security concern, despite continued diplomatic engagement.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil production and limited economic diversification leave the state vulnerable to foreign operators, volatile prices, and external technical capital.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gas-processing and LNG projects remain central to revenue security but depend on foreign investment, technology, and export-market access.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's position on the Red Sea and involvement in regional security dynamics expose its sovereignty to pressure from neighboring states and external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production provides revenue but remains dependent on foreign capital, expertise, and market access, limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, energy, and remittance links with South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union create substantial exposure to external economic conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Diplomatic Recognition Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's continued relationship with Taiwan preserves a distinctive diplomatic channel but can complicate engagement with mainland China and access to some infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's energy sovereignty but continues to generate strategic friction with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and downstream guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Port Access Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Ethiopia's search for reliable maritime access, including arrangements involving Somaliland, faces regional opposition and exposes critical trade infrastructure to geopolitical pressure.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over oil and mining
Diversification remains constrained by external capital

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state control and domestic value capture in oil while remaining dependent on foreign operators, technology, and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Manganese and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mining expansion and rail-port infrastructure create openings for Chinese and other external investors to secure long-term influence over strategic export corridors.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential external partner
Cashew and tourism anchor a narrow resource base

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese interdependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade access, security cooperation, and regional connectivity, limiting policy autonomy despite formal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and agricultural dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited port capacity and dependence on foreign-financed roads, energy, and cashew markets leave the country vulnerable to external commercial and donor priorities.

highlights: Gold remains the strongest sovereign-resource lever

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector informality
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and informal mining damages land and water while enabling illicit financial flows and reducing the state's effective control over gold production.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and critical-minerals pressure
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal dependence on IMF-backed adjustment and foreign investment in lithium, bauxite, and oil constrains Accra's ability to impose stronger local-processing and revenue terms.

highlights: Junta retains tight control over mining negotiations

frictionVectors.title: Simandou consortium dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project offers major state revenue but depends on foreign-led rail, port, and financing arrangements that could lock Guinea into externally controlled export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite sovereignty gap
frictionVectors.details: Guinea is a leading bauxite supplier yet captures limited downstream value, while Chinese and other foreign operators retain significant influence over production and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unprocessed cashew exports leave producers dependent on foreign traders and processors, with weak domestic value addition and limited bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Trafficking and maritime vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and porous maritime routes facilitate narcotics trafficking and external criminal influence, undermining state control over ports and coastal resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and substantial external debt repayments narrow Nairobi's policy space. Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders remain influential in infrastructure and budget decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Lamu corridor are strategic targets for Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests. Emerging competition for Kenya's rare-earth, titanium, and other mineral assets raises concerns over local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but leave Lesotho dependent on Pretoria for project financing, infrastructure, and market access. Expansion of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project may deepen this asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Investment Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The manufacturing base remains exposed to external trade preferences and foreign-owned supply chains. Any shift in US or regional market access could rapidly affect employment and fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining companies remain central to exports, employment, and transport infrastructure, limiting Monrovia's bargaining power over taxation and local processing. Expansion commitments can produce growth while leaving Liberia exposed to commodity-price and corporate decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: Control and modernization of Monrovia's port and mining corridors attract competing foreign commercial interests. Weak domestic logistics capacity increases the risk that infrastructure gains primarily serve export enclaves.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and security authorities continue to contest control over oil revenues, production sites, and the National Oil Corporation. Periodic blockades and institutional fragmentation keep energy sovereignty vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, and other external actors retain influence through military assistance, personnel, and political networks. Their presence complicates reunification and gives outside powers leverage over ports, bases, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Enclave Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining projects are dominated by foreign capital and export markets. Madagascar gains foreign exchange and infrastructure, but domestic processing and fiscal capture remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Chronic power shortages and weak roads constrain national control over production chains and increase reliance on foreign project finance. Competition among Asian, Gulf, and Western investors is growing around ports, logistics, and mineral corridors.

highlights: Critical minerals attract new external capital

frictionVectors.title: External debt and conditional finance
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and creditor negotiations are stabilizing Malawi's finances but limit fiscal room and policy independence. Debt-service pressures continue to shape control over infrastructure and public assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in uranium, rare earths, and other minerals is increasing faster than domestic processing capacity. Malawi risks remaining an exporter of low-value commodities unless contracts and local-content rules improve.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector sovereignty drive
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and stronger control over foreign mining operators. Production disruptions, contract disputes, and weak oversight could reduce investment without guaranteeing broad public benefit.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support has expanded as relations with France and Western partners deteriorate. The arrangement may protect regime security while increasing political, financial, and operational dependence on an external power.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major revenue and diplomatic leverage but remains dependent on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and cross-border coordination with Senegal. Local-content and revenue-transparency gaps could limit sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and corridor concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and transport infrastructure remain closely tied to foreign markets and a narrow set of operators. Price volatility, port dependence, and insecurity along Sahel trade routes expose Mauritania to external shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and maritime jurisdiction
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos settlement and future control arrangements remain central to Mauritius's sovereignty claims and maritime-resource access. Strategic competition around Diego Garcia gives external powers considerable leverage over the outcome.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and port competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius must balance Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf commercial interests in ports, logistics, and digital infrastructure. Competition can expand national capacity but creates exposure to strategic alignment pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and investment in Western Sahara underpin its resource and infrastructure strategy but remain contested by the Polisario Front and Algeria. Foreign firms face legal and reputational risks when operating in the territory.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, renewable energy, rail, and automotive supply chains attract substantial European, Gulf, Chinese, and American investment. Rabat retains significant leverage, but dependence on external technology and markets can constrain strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency Threat to LNG Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence in Cabo Delgado continues to threaten logistics, local communities, and the timetable for offshore gas development. Security dependence on foreign partners limits Maputo's operational autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Gas Value Chain
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders remain central to financing, technology, and marketing for Mozambique's LNG sector. The government is seeking greater domestic content and revenue capture without deterring project reactivation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Major Control of Offshore Discoveries
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore oil and gas discoveries have increased Namibia's leverage but also its dependence on international majors for exploration, capital, and technical capacity. Negotiations over fiscal terms and local participation will shape sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen and mineral projects require major external investment in ports, power, water, and transport corridors. Windhoek is balancing rapid development against concerns over land, employment, and foreign ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Contract Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are using resource nationalism to renegotiate or challenge foreign mining interests, especially in uranium. This may increase state control but risks reduced investment, technical disruption, and export losses.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The rupture with former Western security partners has pushed Niger toward new external relationships, including Russia, while border insecurity remains severe. Sovereignty gains are constrained by dependence on outside military support and fragile transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Contract Friction
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is seeking new upstream investment while asserting tighter regulatory and fiscal control through petroleum-sector reforms. Disputes over contracts, taxation, and local-content obligations continue to complicate cooperation with international producers.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Export Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and insecurity in the Niger Delta reduce public revenue and weaken state control over production corridors. Refining expansion improves domestic resilience but remains exposed to supply, power, and logistics bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and DRC Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role as a transit and trading hub for minerals, particularly from the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, faces sustained international scrutiny. Sanctions risk and diplomatic pressure could constrain access to markets, finance, and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Security Partnerships and Sovereignty Costs
frictionVectors.details: Kigali's regional military influence provides strategic leverage but generates friction with the DRC, neighboring states, and Western partners. External aid and investment remain important, leaving Rwanda exposed to conditionality linked to conflict conduct.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION
frictionVectors.details: Unproven hydrocarbon prospects attract foreign firms while São Tomé and Príncipe lacks the capital and technical capacity to manage exploration independently. Future licensing could create sovereignty and revenue-sharing disputes.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCING DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support remain reliant on partners including Portugal, China, and multilateral lenders. This expands policy options but limits autonomous control over strategic projects.

highlights: Resource nationalism meets first gas revenues

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND GAS CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national value capture and review of legacy arrangements as offshore production expands. Tensions with international operators and lenders could affect investment confidence and project timelines.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, rail, and energy infrastructure remains central to Senegal's growth strategy. Competition among European, Gulf, Chinese, and Turkish actors creates leverage risks around critical trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME DOMAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on external partners for maritime surveillance, anti-piracy operations, and enforcement across its large exclusive economic zone. This constrains fully autonomous control over fisheries and offshore activity.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM AND INFRASTRUCTURE OWNERSHIP
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital dominates much of the high-value tourism and infrastructure economy. The government retains regulatory authority but remains exposed to external financing, imported energy, and demand shocks.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINING TERMS
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mineral projects generate export income but leave Sierra Leone exposed to foreign capital, commodity cycles, and disputes over taxation, local processing, and environmental obligations. Government efforts to improve domestic value capture face strong investor pressure.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and resource-linked investment remain important to transport and industrial development. Debt, procurement transparency, and long-term control of strategic assets remain recurring sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL LICENSING
frictionVectors.details: Federal efforts to develop offshore hydrocarbons are constrained by disputes with member states, limited administrative capacity, and insecurity. Foreign operators and partners may gain disproportionate leverage before Somalia establishes robust regulatory institutions.

frictionVectors.title: SECURITY AND PORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Somalia relies heavily on foreign military, financial, and technical support to secure ports, shipping lanes, and resource zones. Turkish, Gulf, Western, and regional involvement strengthens capacity while complicating unified national control.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and grid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent Eskom financial, generation, and transmission constraints limit industrial sovereignty and raise reliance on private-sector investment and imported energy inputs.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for battery and platinum-group mineral access, while South Africa seeks greater local processing and beneficiation.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the state’s lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on pipelines and export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving sovereign revenue exposed to conflict, outages, and bargaining pressure from external transit actors.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and foreign resource capture
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and opaque oil contracting constrain public control over hydrocarbons, while neighboring states and international firms retain strong leverage over logistics and finance.

highlights: Red Sea access is strategically contested

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gold war economy
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and commercial networks control parts of Sudan’s gold, oil, and agricultural systems, enabling outside financing and reducing civilian sovereignty over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea coast, Port Sudan, and overland supply routes are exposed to regional power competition, with infrastructure access increasingly tied to military and diplomatic influence.

highlights: Gas and minerals policy is more assertive

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic corridors
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and logistics projects involving Gulf, Chinese, European, and other investors expand connectivity but create long-term leverage over trade routes and concession terms.

frictionVectors.title: Resource nationalism versus investment
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater state participation and domestic processing in natural gas and critical minerals, creating periodic tension with multinational investors over fiscal terms and local content.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Togo’s fiscal and strategic position relies heavily on the Port of Lomé and foreign-backed logistics networks, leaving customs revenue and connectivity vulnerable to external commercial influence.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover and security assistance
frictionVectors.details: Militant pressure from Burkina Faso and the wider Sahel is increasing demand for external security support, which can constrain national autonomy and redirect scarce resources toward border defense.

highlights: Phosphate and port assets remain strategic

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding, trade access, and migration cooperation give Brussels substantial influence over Tunisia’s fiscal and security choices. Debt pressures limit Tunis’s room to reject externally conditioned support.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and dependence on imported hydrocarbons expose Tunisia to price shocks and external supply pressure, particularly from Algeria and European markets.

highlights: Oil corridor locks in external partnerships
Regional logistics remain a strategic asset

frictionVectors.title: EACOP and foreign-led oil development
frictionVectors.details: The Lake Albert oil project and EACOP are dominated by foreign energy and finance partners, creating revenue, environmental, and sovereignty disputes. Uganda retains state participation but faces limited control over technology, capital, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Regional corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uganda depends heavily on Kenyan and Tanzanian transport corridors for fuel and future oil exports. Border disruptions or bilateral disputes could quickly affect national energy security.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: International firms still dominate major mines, refining capacity, and technology, leaving Zambia exposed to decisions made outside the country. Lusaka is pressing for greater local processing and state participation without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: US-China competition over critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is leveraging Western and Chinese interest in copper and cobalt infrastructure, including transport links and processing. Competing offers create bargaining power but also pressure Zambia to align strategically.

highlights: Lithium and platinum draw competing patrons

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance of strategic mining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, South African, and other foreign investors remain central to lithium, platinum, gold, and chrome production. Export controls and beneficiation rules have increased state leverage, but financing and technical dependence persist.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and infrastructure bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, unreliable electricity, and constrained payment channels raise the cost of independent resource development. Power shortages and rail limitations push producers toward foreign-controlled logistics and energy arrangements.
